title: Faceless running isn't inelegant—it's the optimum reinforcement learning selected
dek: To run faster, Tiangong (天工) Omni automatically abandoned the human intuition of arm-swing balance, instead using waist rotation—the solution the machine learned may not look elegant, but it obeys the physics-constrained optimum.
why: Want to know what embodied AI companies really mean when they talk about emergence, open-source, and 'national team'—this episode has straight talk from someone on the front lines, not PR speak.
who: Investors and founders focused on embodied AI and robotics, plus anyone trying to understand the open-source dynamics between 'national team' labs and commercial companies.
skip: 0:00–2:01 is intro and small talk; skip straight to the technical breakdown of faceless running.

points.h: Punishment functions forced reinforcement learning to innovate a new gait
points.body: Faceless running was not designed—it emerged from the training setup. The team deliberately restricted the robot's shoulder-joint rotation angles to block the intuitive balancing strategy of arm swing. To run fast while maintaining balance under these constraints, the robot trained itself into a different running style using waist rotation instead. Xiong Youjun calls this a rare moment of emergence in embodied AI: the optimization process discovered a solution the team had not conceived.

points.h: Nobody knows how much data embodied-AI scaling laws will actually require
points.body: Tiangong trained its universal motion controller on several hundred hours of human motion capture; NVIDIA's Sonic controller used roughly 700+ hours—comparable scale. But when asked how much data embodied AI's scaling law will need, Xiong freely admits the field doesn't know yet. The gap between current data (hundreds of hours) and plausible requirements (millions of hours) is still orders of magnitude. More provocatively, he doubts whether stacking data alone is even the right path—large language models work this way because the internet supplies infinite text, but embodied AI may need a different learning paradigm, closer to how human children explore and fail.

points.h: The industry jumped to full autonomy in a single year, and computing power drove it
points.body: Last year's marathon race fielded 200+ robots; only Tiangong ran fully autonomously; the rest relied on human teleoperation for guidance. This year, most competitors achieved autonomy in all but the occasional obstacle course. Xiong attributes this shift not to accumulated time but to concentrated investment: the entire industry shifted resources and talent toward robot brains—perception, decision-making, learned control. The payoff came fast.

points.h: Fewer than five independent startups have the compute to train embodied-AI brains
points.body: The episode explores an industry claim: outside of government labs and Big Tech, fewer than five venture-backed companies have enough compute to train large brain models. Xiong did not dispute this. He acknowledged that training an embodied AI brain demands extreme computational resources. Tiangong draws on Baidu's cloud infrastructure and their own data-collection centers, which now hold nearly 200,000 hours of high-quality egocentric footage—a rare advantage.

points.h: Honda's 2000s robotics paradigm became obsolete when deep learning arrived
points.body: Xiong's passion for robotics traces to 2002: a video of Honda's P2 (the ancestor of ASIMO) escorting a Chinese leader through a factory. The vision was electric—human-robot collaboration would define the future. But Honda's entire approach rested on mathematical models, not learning. The robot carried a heavy external compute backpack and had weak strategic reasoning and vision. When deep learning and large language models emerged, that entire technical architecture became obsolete overnight—a Nokia moment for Honda, which lost its pole position in humanoid robotics.

points.h: High-level teleoperation delegates human judgment to machines without replacing thought
points.body: Some competitors lost their entries for lying about autonomy while relying on teleoperation. Yet the rules explicitly permit teleoperation because it operates at different levels. Framewise puppet control is one thing; task-level teleoperation is another. A human can tell the robot a complex goal—eg, "check if that breaker should be flipped"—and the robot decides its own path, navigation, obstacles, and execution. This is collaboration between human judgment and machine capability, not evasion.

points.h: National-team KPIs optimize for industry breakthroughs, not commercial returns
points.body: Xiong's move from CTO at Ubtech to head of the Robotics Innovation Center was a shift from company to country: from maximizing commercial gain to finding shared friction across the whole industry. The center has released the Tiangong robots, Huisi Awakening software, and other foundational work as open-source, so that commercial companies don't duplicate low-level infrastructure and waste social resources. The early shareholders—Ubtech, Xiaomi, Yizhuang State-owned Capital—were not chasing returns; they were betting on the technical direction itself.

points.h: Every sensor reading introduces irreversible error that caps robot precision
points.body: Large language models work with purely digital I/O: text in, tokens out, negligible loss. Robots are different. Each input—vision, touch, force—and each motor command introduces noise and drift. Unlike software, these errors compound and cannot be fully corrected. Precision degrades with every physical interaction. Xiong confirmed this bottleneck and framed the solution: unify different modalities—vision, language, touch—into a single learned representation space, then reason and act from that shared substrate. This unified model, called Pelican Unified, is what his team is now building.

terms.def: Vision-Language-Action model—end-to-end robot control that unifies visual perception, language understanding, and motor output in a single neural network
First-person video footage from cameras worn by human operators, used to train robots through imitation learning at low cost
A learned model that lets robots internally predict and reason about physical cause-and-effect in their environment
A single representation space that fuses VLA, multimodal LLM, and world-model capabilities into one coherent reasoning system
The principle that model performance improves predictably with greater data and compute—proven for LLMs, still unverified for embodied AI

quotes.text: We deliberately restricted shoulder-joint rotation angles. To run that fast while maintaining balance, the robot trained itself into a new gait. It's genuine self-learning and self-evolution.
We've always thought that relying purely on data collection might not be the right approach.
Our data collection volume today is already quite large—the first-person footage alone is approaching 200,000 hours—and it's high-quality data.
Different modalities' signal representations introduce losses, so we're now pursuing unified representation across all modalities.
Robots that don't meet safety standards cannot be sold. Otherwise they might cause unnecessary harm to society and users. It's a fundamental bottom line.
